title: What are the three forms of JPA projections (interface-based, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic), how does each work, and when do you use which?
shortTitle: Interface, class/DTO constructor, dynamic generic projections?
keyPoints: Interface projection declares getter methods and Spring builds a JDK proxy at runtime, narrowing the SQL for closed projections.
DTO/class projection uses a JPQL constructor expression or a Java record, producing plain unmanaged objects with no proxy overhead.
Dynamic projection takes a Class<T> parameter so one repository method returns different shapes at runtime.
Closed interface projections narrow the SQL to declared getters; open projections with @Value SpEL load the full entity first.
DTO projection is the fastest because it skips both the persistence context and the proxy layer.
Nested interface projections across associations can silently fire N+1 queries unless the underlying query uses JOIN FETCH.

s1_definition.oneliner: Interface projection is a proxy over selected getters, DTO/class projection is a constructor expression or record (fastest), and dynamic projection takes a Class<T> so the caller chooses the shape at runtime.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Interface projection** – a plain Java interface with getter methods matching entity properties; Spring Data builds a JDK proxy backed by only those columns.
- **Closed projection** – an interface projection where every getter maps directly to a property, allowing SQL column narrowing.
- **Open projection** – an interface projection using @Value SpEL that can reference any property, forcing Hibernate to load the full entity first.
- **DTO/class projection** – a JPQL constructor expression (`SELECT new ...`) or a Java record that produces an immutable, unmanaged object.
- **Dynamic projection** – a generic repository method with a `Class<T>` parameter so the caller picks the shape at runtime.
- **Performance ranking** – DTO (fastest, no proxy, no PC) > closed interface (fast, small proxy cost) > full entity (slowest, managed, snapshots).
s1_definition.analogy: Rajesh asks National Bank of India for his fixed-deposit details. The interface projection is a clerk who photocopies only the two lines you asked for onto a slip. The DTO projection is a clerk who hands you a pre-printed receipt with exactly those fields already laid out. The dynamic projection is a clerk who asks which format would you like today and prints whichever one you name at the counter.

sections.s3_flow:
```text
  Three Projection Forms
  ============================================

  1. Interface Projection (Closed)
     Repository method returns: List<FdSummary>
     +---------------------------+
     | SELECT fd_id, maturity_amt|  <- only declared getters
     |           |               |
     |           v               |
     |    JDK Dynamic Proxy      |  <- Spring builds at runtime
     |    implements FdSummary   |
     |    (not managed)          |
     +---------------------------+

  2. DTO/Class Projection
     Repository method returns: List<FdDto>
     +---------------------------+
     | SELECT fd_id, maturity_amt|  <- constructor params
     |           |               |
     |           v               |
     |    new FdDto(id, amount)  |  <- plain record
     |    (no proxy, no PC)      |
     +---------------------------+

  3. Dynamic Projection
     Repository method: <T> List<T> findBy(..., Class<T>)
     +---------------------------+
     |  Class<T> type parameter  |
     |           |               |
     |    FdSummary.class?       |---> Interface proxy (narrow SQL)
     |    FdDto.class?           |---> Record object (narrow SQL)
     |    FixedDeposit.class?    |---> Full entity (SELECT *)
     +---------------------------+

  Performance: DTO > Interface (closed) > Entity
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
JPA projections let Rajesh fetch only the data a screen actually needs instead of hydrating a full entity, and Spring Data gives three forms. The interface-based projection is a plain Java interface with getters; Spring Data builds a proxy and, for a closed projection, narrows the SQL to just those columns. The DTO projection uses a JPQL constructor expression or a record return type; this is the fastest form because the objects never enter the persistence context and there is no proxy. The dynamic projection declares a single finder with a generic type parameter and a Class argument, so the caller decides at runtime whether to get a lightweight interface, a DTO, or the full entity from one method.

In the fixed-deposit portal at National Bank of India, the summary list uses a closed interface projection that reads only the deposit id and maturity amount, two columns instead of twelve. The detail API uses a DTO constructor projection so the JSON contract is explicit and there are no lazy-proxy serialization surprises. The search screen uses a dynamic projection so the same query powers both a compact row and a full drill-down depending on a toggle.

The performance ordering Pankaj keeps in mind is that the DTO projection is fastest because it reads the fewest columns and skips persistence-context management, the closed interface projection is close behind with a small proxy cost, and the full entity is slowest because every row carries a snapshot for dirty checking. The senior caution is that nested interface projections across associations can quietly trigger an extra query per row, so keep projections flat and move to a DTO whenever you need computed or joined values.

Remember one sentence: interface projections build proxies, DTO projections build plain records with no overhead, and dynamic projections let the caller choose the shape at runtime.
